clue.text: Keep limb bony — OK in contest?

definitions.text: Keep limb bony — OK in contest?

indicators.note: the question mark is the only signal, warning that the whole clue's letters must be rearranged rather than read

parts.words: Keep limb bony — OK in contest
parts.note: every letter of the clue is the raw material

explanation.surface: Advice to a contestant at a seaside show: keep that leg bony and you'll do fine.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram word at all: the twenty-three letters of the clue rearrange into the answer, and the whole clue also describes it. A knobbly knees competition is an old British holiday-camp contest judging men's bony knees.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a contest rewards exactly a bony leg joint, so keeping a limb bony is how a competitor would succeed there.

clue.text: Put it on to stop most of family nonsense

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept

parts.note: kin are one's relatives
bosh is a dated word for rubbish talk

explanation.surface: Someone stops a family squabble by declaring it all nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the idiom 'put the kibosh on', meaning to halt something; 'it' stands for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In the set phrase, putting the kibosh on a plan means quashing or ending it, so this is the thing you put on to stop.

clue.text: Nothing clear confused seer

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled up and must be put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller whose vision is anything but clear.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a prophet or priestess giving predictions, the same role as a seer who foretells events.

clue.text: Mad support follows from fields first

parts.note: bats is slang for crazy
to second a motion is to back it

explanation.surface: A crazy backer emerges straight out of the fields.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cricket: the team that fields first has its turn at the crease second, so that outcome follows.
explanation.definitionFit: In a two-innings cricket match, a side that takes the field first necessarily takes its turn at the wicket afterwards.

clue.text: City careerist raised money during the years

indicators.note: something happening during the years sits inside that span, so the pieces go within

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, doubled for the plural
raised means up
p for pence, small change

explanation.surface: A young banker who has made a pile of money over the years.
explanation.definitionFit: A yuppie is a young urban professional, the stereotypical ambitious worker in the City, London's financial district.

clue.text: Deformed vampire, death and hell, not he; stakes a speciality!

indicators.note: something deformed has been bent out of its proper shape, so the letters lose their order
'not he' tells us to take those two letters away from the words before them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove from hell

explanation.surface: A horror-film pitch: a twisted vampire, death and hell, with stakes as the special feature.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing HE from HELL leaves LL; mix that with VAMPIRE and DEATH to get the name. The stakes are wooden posts, not wagers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wallachian prince Vlad III was notorious for executing enemies by impaling them on sharpened wooden posts, his gruesome hallmark.

clue.text: Indecision seen forming in cranial nerve

indicators.note: forming something new means the letters are reshaped into a different word

parts.note: taken as written
the vagus is the tenth cranial nerve

explanation.surface: A doctor notices a dithering patient's problem lies in a nerve in the head.
explanation.walkthrough: The anatomy knowledge is the hard part: the vagus nerve runs from the brain stem to the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: Vagueness is a lack of firmness or clarity of mind, which shows itself as dithering and inability to decide.

clue.text: Book of information without introduction

indicators.note: without its introduction the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: facts are pieces of information

explanation.surface: A reference book full of data but lacking a preface.
explanation.definitionFit: Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament, usually shortened to its first word.

clue.text: Reptile and one fish in net hauled up

indicators.note: in a down entry, hauling something up makes it read from bottom to top
one thing in another sits inside it, so the first pieces go within the net

parts.note: taken as written; it holds the next two pieces
Roman numeral one
a parr is a young salmon

explanation.surface: A fisherman pulls up his net to find a reptile and a fish inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, a reptile of ponds and rivers.

clue.text: Editing the denouement to grab me

indicators.note: to grab something is to hold it, so the denouement word wraps round the other

parts.note: a denouement is the ending of a story
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer reworking a final chapter so it seizes the reader.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct and improve it, which is the work of an editor revising a manuscript.

clue.text: Gust of wind, blow!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sudden strong rush of air
second meaning: a mild curse of annoyance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like part of the weather, but with the exclamation mark it is the expletive 'Blow!', meaning damn.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a powerful burst of air and is also an exclamation of irritation, just as 'blow it!' is.

clue.text: Sun's exposure

parts.note: surface reading: time spent in sunshine, as in sunbathing
setter's reading: the person the Sun newspaper put on display

explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid that for decades printed a topless model on an inside page; 'exposure' is both sunlight and baring skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The topless model in that tabloid was literally exposed to readers, so she was the paper's exposure in a second sense.

clue.text: Fly sets off, guided in its own image?

indicators.note: when something goes off it goes wrong, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
led means guided

explanation.surface: An insect takes off and is steered along, perhaps in a likeness of itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Something self-styled is described or fashioned by its own account, so it is made after its own picture of itself.

clue.text: Song without "la" is smooth on top

indicators.note: without the quoted syllable means those letters are taken out of the song word

parts.note: a ballad is a narrative song
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A tune with no 'la' in it, sung by someone with a shiny head.
explanation.definitionFit: A head with no hair is slick and hairless at the crown, which is what this adjective describes.

clue.text: Boar hunter takes the filth to heart

parts.note: the filth and pigs are both British slang for the police
ticker is slang for the heart

explanation.surface: A hunter of wild boar is upset by the mud and dirt of the chase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes to heart' wants to be one idiom, but heart is a piece of its own; the filth is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Pig-sticking was the colonial sport of hunting wild boar on horseback with a spear, and a pig-sticker is one who practises it.

clue.text: See 1
One will remember Scrooge storing up capital

indicators.note: something storing another holds it inside, so the capital goes within the Scrooge word

parts.note: Scrooge is the archetypal skinflint

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the capital reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the capital of Italy

explanation.surface: Scrooge hoarding money, a tale that someone will surely recall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts as money for a miser to store, but here it is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A memoriser is a person who learns things by heart, so it is someone who will remember.

clue.text: Seasoned beef as "Armpit Stew"

indicators.note: a stew is a mixture cooked together, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deli's spiced beef mocked as tasting like an armpit stew.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is cured brisket rubbed with spices such as pepper and coriander, then smoked, a classic seasoned meat.

clue.text: Ends relationship, so begins the holidays

definitions.meaning: first meaning: splits from a partner
second meaning: what a British school does on the last day of term

explanation.surface: Someone dumps their partner just as their free time starts.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a school is said to break up when term ends and the holidays begin.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both separating from a lover and, for a school, closing at the end of term.

clue.text: Cultivating grain, so most expert in their field?

indicators.note: cultivating means working the soil, turning it over, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: Farmers growing cereals, the most skilled of their kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Field' is literal here: these are experts in arable land, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Agronomists are scientists of soil and crop production, so their specialist area is quite literally farmland.

clue.text: Where camping is determined?

explanation.surface: A question about how a campsite pitch gets decided.
explanation.definitionFit: Intent as an adjective means resolved or set on a purpose, a synonym of firmly decided.

clue.text: Nick for rogue trader?

parts.note: surface reading: a prison cell for a crooked dealer, nick being jail
setter's reading: Nick is the first name, and we want the surname of the notorious rogue trader

explanation.walkthrough: Nick is British slang for prison, which fits a fraudster; but it is a first name. Nick Leeson's unauthorised dealing broke Barings Bank in 1995.
explanation.definitionFit: The trader whose hidden losses collapsed Barings Bank was Nick Leeson, so his surname completes the name.

clue.text: Gin finds the mouth

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a snare for catching animals
second meaning: slang for the mouth

explanation.surface: A drink of gin making its way to someone's lips.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin is not the spirit but a gin trap, a spring snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin is a type of snare for animals, and the same word is colloquial for a person's mouth.

clue.text: Clairvoyance reveals ghost around the Channel Islands

indicators.note: one thing around another encloses it, so the ghost word wraps the islands

parts.note: a presence is a felt spirit or ghost
CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands

explanation.surface: A psychic senses a spirit haunting Jersey and Guernsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Prescience is foreknowledge of events before they happen, the gift a clairvoyant claims to have.

clue.text: Abrupt and unreasonable

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rising or falling sharply, as a slope
second meaning: excessive, as in a price that is too much

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like descriptions of a rude person, but one is about gradient and the other about cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a sharp incline and, colloquially, a demand or price that is excessively high.

clue.text: See 10
'x' co-ordinates make BASIC essay wrong, not 'y'

indicators.note: letters gone wrong are out of their correct order and need rearranging
not with a quoted letter means that letter is dropped from the fodder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; its y is the letter to remove

explanation.surface: A student's essay on the programming language BASIC gets its graph axes mixed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'x' and 'y' sound like algebra, and one is; the other is just a letter of essay.
explanation.definitionFit: On a graph, an abscissa is a point's horizontal distance from the origin, its x value; this is the plural.

clue.text: See 1
See 5
Moralist girl entertained by joke

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is held within the host's home, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a pun is a play on words
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A strait-laced person's daughter is amused by a quip.
explanation.definitionFit: A puritan is someone with strict moral or religious principles, who disapproves of pleasure.
